vignette:
Sophea Meas was eighty years old, a wife, a mother, and a grandmother, and for decades she had been the quiet, steady heart of her community’s temple education program. She taught children the old stories, the chants, the rituals of respect. She had lived through the killing fields of Cambodia as a young woman, and she had built a life in America that she believed had finally buried that past. But the past, she had learned, does not stay buried. It rises through the soil.

The event that had fractured her life was not a single moment but a season of terror. In 1975, when the Khmer Rouge took Phnom Penh, Sophea was forced from her home and marched into the countryside. She was twenty-nine. She spent four years in a labor camp, where she watched her husband at the time die of starvation, where she was beaten for praying, where she was made to dig graves for strangers and friends alike. The memory that now consumed her most was not the largest atrocity but a specific, small horror. One evening, she was ordered to burn a pile of clothing taken from executed prisoners. As the flames rose, a soldier shoved her forward without warning—his hand flat against her back, hard enough to make her stumble. She fell into the edge of the fire. The smell of her own burning sleeve, the heat on her arm, the shouts, the laughter of the guards—these fragments had become the architecture of her waking life.

Now, eighty years old and safe in a tidy suburban home, Sophea could not walk into her own backyard without her heart seizing. The smell of damp earth, of turned soil, of the garden her husband had planted—it was the same smell as the camp. She had stopped going outside entirely. When her grandson ran to hug her from behind, she screamed. She had come to believe, with a certainty that shamed her, that her body was no longer her own. She could not trust it to stay calm, to stay still, to not betray her. She felt that something intrinsic in her—some weakness, some failing—had made the soldier push her that day. She had been too slow, too afraid, too soft. The humiliation of that moment had calcified into a permanent, silent shame. She could not speak of it, not even to her current husband of forty years.

The memory itself was strange to her. There were gaps—she could not remember how she got back to her hut that night, or who helped her, or if anyone did. The memory felt alien, as though it had happened to a different woman, a woman she pitied but did not recognize. Yet it was also more real than the present. When she closed her eyes, the fire was brighter than the lamp on her nightstand. The smell was stronger than the jasmine incense she burned each morning.

To survive, Sophea had built a set of rituals. She checked the locks on every door and window three times before bed, and once more before dawn. She kept her mind occupied constantly—reciting chants, counting breaths, listening to talk radio at a volume that filled the silence. And she had stopped making new friends. After a woman at the temple invited her to a gardening club, Sophea had politely declined, then avoided the temple for two months. She could not explain why. She only knew that the thought of sitting in someone’s backyard, of smelling soil, of being touched unexpectedly by a friendly hand on the shoulder—it was not worth the risk. Her world had shrunk to the interior of her house, to the same three chairs, to the same television programs.

What finally brought her to a clinic was a small incident that broke through her defenses. Her husband had lit a candle for the evening prayer, and the flame had flickered. She had frozen, then wept, then told him, for the first time in forty years, that she could not keep living this way. She was terrified of what therapy might ask of her—of having to remember more, to feel more, to admit that her body and her history were not separate. But she was also, beneath the fear, hoping for something she could barely name: that the soil in her garden might one day smell only like soil.
